questions.stem: Which of the following best defines contribution per unit?
options: Selling price per unit less variable cost per unit
Selling price per unit less total cost per unit
Total revenue less total fixed costs
Profit per unit after all costs
questions.why: Contribution is what each unit contributes towards covering fixed costs and then towards profit.
whyNot: That is profit per unit under absorption costing.
That is not a standard measure.
Profit per unit is contribution less fixed cost per unit.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a semi-variable cost?
options: A cost with both a fixed element and a variable element
A cost that is fixed over a range of output and then steps up
A cost that changes in direct proportion to output
A cost that does not change with output
questions.why: A standing charge plus a usage charge is the classic example, and it must be split before use.
whyNot: That is a semi-fixed or stepped cost.
That is a variable cost.
That is a fixed cost.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the margin of safety?
options: The amount by which actual or planned output exceeds the break-even output
The difference between selling price and variable cost
The level of output at which no profit or loss is made
The profit made at the current level of output
questions.why: It measures how far output can fall before the business moves into loss, so it is a measure of risk.
whyNot: That is contribution per unit.
That is the break-even point.
That is profit.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the angle of incidence?
options: The angle between the total revenue and total cost lines at the break-even point
The angle of the fixed cost line on the chart
The angle between the two axes of the chart
The slope of the variable cost line
questions.why: A wide angle means profit grows quickly beyond break-even, which reflects a high contribution to sales ratio.
whyNot: The fixed cost line is horizontal.
The axes are always at right angles.
The slope of a line is not an angle of incidence.

questions.stem: Selling price is $45 and variable costs are materials $16, labour $9 and variable overhead $5. What is contribution per unit?
questions.why: Variable cost = 16 + 9 + 5 = $30. Contribution = 45 - 30 = $15.
whyNot: That is the variable cost per unit.
That omits the variable overhead.
That omits the labour cost.

questions.stem: Fixed costs are $180,000 and contribution per unit is $15. What is the break-even output?
options: 12,000 units
4,000 units
6,000 units
questions.why: Break-even = 180,000 / 15 = 12,000 units.
whyNot: That divides by the selling price of $45 instead of contribution.
That multiplies the two figures.
That divides by $30, the variable cost.

questions.stem: Contribution per unit is $15 and the selling price is $45. What is the contribution to sales ratio?
whyNot: That is the variable cost to sales ratio.
That inverts the ratio.
That misplaces the decimal point.

questions.stem: Fixed costs are $180,000 and the contribution to sales ratio is 33.3%. What is break-even revenue?
whyNot: That multiplies rather than divides.
That is the fixed cost figure.
That is break-even in units, not revenue.

questions.stem: Break-even output is 12,000 units and actual output is 14,000 units. What is the margin of safety as a percentage?
questions.why: (14,000 - 12,000) / 14,000 x 100 = 14.3%. The percentage is taken on actual output.
whyNot: That divides by the break-even output rather than actual output.
That is the break-even output as a percentage of actual.
That misplaces the decimal point.

questions.stem: Contribution per unit is $15, fixed costs are $180,000 and 14,000 units are sold. What is the profit?
whyNot: That is total contribution, before deducting fixed costs.
That is the fixed cost figure.
That adds the fixed costs instead of deducting them.

questions.stem: Fixed costs are $180,000, contribution per unit is $15 and the target profit is $75,000. What output is needed?
options: 17,000 units
5,000 units
12,000 units
19,000 units
whyNot: That covers only the target profit and ignores the fixed costs.
That is the break-even output with no target profit.
That uses an incorrect calculation.

questions.stem: Maintenance cost was $34,000 at 9,000 units and $46,000 at 15,000 units. What is the variable cost per unit?
whyNot: That divides the total cost by the units at one level.
That uses an incorrect denominator.
That is the total cost difference in thousands, not the rate.

questions.stem: Using the figures above, what is the fixed element of the maintenance cost?
questions.why: At 9,000 units the variable part is 9,000 x 2.00 = $18,000, so the fixed element is 34,000 - 18,000 = $16,000. Check at 15,000: 16,000 + 30,000 = $46,000.
whyNot: That is the variable element at 9,000 units.
That is the total cost at the lower level.
That is the difference in total costs.

questions.stem: A business has high fixed costs and contribution of $15 per unit. Output rises 10% from 14,000 to 15,400 units. What happens to profit?
options: It rises from $30,000 to $51,000, a rise of 70%
It rises by 10%, in line with output
It rises from $30,000 to $33,000
It falls, because fixed costs rise with output
questions.why: 1,400 extra units x $15 = $21,000 extra profit on a base of $30,000. High fixed costs magnify movements in both directions.
whyNot: Profit does not move in proportion to output once fixed costs are covered.
That applies 10% to the profit rather than adding the extra contribution.
Fixed costs do not rise with output within the relevant range.

questions.stem: Why is a break-even point calculated beyond the next step in a stepped fixed cost invalid?
options: Fixed costs will have risen, so the figure used in the calculation is wrong
Contribution per unit changes at every step
The selling price must fall at higher volumes
Break-even analysis cannot be used with stepped costs at all
questions.why: Each step changes the fixed cost total, which invalidates a break-even figure calculated with the earlier total.
whyNot: Contribution per unit is unaffected by fixed costs.
There is no necessary connection between volume and price here.
It can be used within each relevant range.

questions.stem: On a break-even chart, where does the sales revenue line start?
options: At the origin, because no sales means no revenue
At the fixed cost level on the vertical axis
At the break-even point
At the total cost line
questions.why: Revenue is zero at zero output, whereas the total cost line starts at the fixed cost level because those costs are incurred anyway.
whyNot: That is where the total cost line starts.
The break-even point is where the two lines cross, not where revenue begins.
The two lines are separate.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of break-even analysis?
options: It assumes all output is sold, so it ignores inventory
It cannot be used for a single-product business
It requires a discount rate to be estimated
It cannot allow for fixed costs
questions.why: It also assumes linear costs and revenue, one selling price and constant fixed costs, all of which are simplifications.
whyNot: A single product is precisely the case it suits best.
There is no discounting in break-even analysis.
Fixed costs are central to the calculation.

questions.stem: What happens to fixed cost per unit as output rises?
options: It falls, which is where economies of scale come from
It rises, because total fixed costs rise
It stays the same
It falls to zero at break-even
questions.why: Total fixed costs are unchanged, so spreading them over more units reduces the cost per unit.
whyNot: Total fixed costs do not rise with output within the relevant range.
Variable cost per unit stays the same; fixed cost per unit does not.
It never reaches zero.

questions.stem: A company's margin of safety is 14.3% and its sales are highly seasonal. What is the appropriate judgement?
options: The margin is uncomfortably thin, because a modest fall in demand would wipe out the profit
The margin is comfortable, because it is positive
The margin is irrelevant where sales are seasonal
The margin should be compared with the contribution to sales ratio
questions.why: Whether a margin of safety is adequate depends on how volatile demand is, which is exactly the kind of conditional judgement that earns marks.
whyNot: Being positive is the minimum, not a sign of comfort.
Volatile demand makes the margin more important, not less.
They measure different things and are not directly comparable.

questions.stem: The selling price is increased. What must be done to find the new break-even point?
options: Recalculate contribution per unit first, then divide fixed costs by it
Reduce the old break-even figure in proportion to the price rise
Divide the old break-even figure by the new price
Nothing, because break-even depends only on fixed costs
questions.why: Every other formula depends on contribution, so the contribution must be recalculated before anything else.
whyNot: Adjusting the old figure proportionally does not work.
That has no arithmetic basis.
Break-even depends on contribution as well as fixed costs.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a semi-fixed cost?
options: A cost that is fixed over a range of output and then steps up to a new level
A cost with a fixed element and a variable element per unit
A cost that is half fixed and half variable
A cost that varies with output but not in direct proportion
questions.why: Employing one supervisor per 20 workers is the standard example, and each step changes total fixed costs.
whyNot: That is a semi-variable cost.
The split is not necessarily equal, and this is not the definition.
That describes a non-linear cost, not a stepped one.
